canonicalExplanation.summary: When you call an **instance method** through a reference, Java picks the implementation from the **actual object's class at run time**: `Shape s = new Circle(2); s.area();` runs **Circle's** area. That's **dynamic dispatch**, and it's what makes polymorphism work. But not everything dispatches dynamically. **Overloads** are chosen at compile time from declared types. **Static methods** and **fields** are resolved by the declared type, and **private** methods can't be overridden. Always write **`@Override`**: if the signature doesn't actually override (a typo, wrong parameter type), the compiler reports it instead of silently creating a new method.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner writes `public boolean equals(Circle other)` in Circle, expecting HashSet to use it, and duplicates keep appearing. The method **overloads** equals(Object) instead of overriding it. Separately, `Shape s = new Circle(2)` correctly calls Circle's area. A Shape reference holding a Circle invokes Circle.area at runtime, and @Override lets the compiler verify the intended signature. In this lesson you'll trace polymorphic calls and repair an accidental non-override.


sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Constructors and invariants**, **Class inheritance** and **Overloading and local scope** (compile-time overload choice).

sections.heading: The rule: overrides dispatch at run time, other things don't
@Override as a safety net

includes: Trace dynamic dispatch of overridden methods through base references.
Distinguish overrides from overloads, statics and fields, and use @Override to catch non-overrides.

outcomes: Trace polymorphic calls and repair an accidental non-override.

examples.title: A Shape reference holding a Circle
examples.situation: A Shape reference holding a Circle invokes Circle.area at runtime, and @Override lets the compiler verify the intended signature.
walkthrough: **A Shape reference holding a Circle invokes Circle.area at runtime:** s.area() prints 12.57.
**@Override lets the compiler verify the intended signature:** equals(Circle) marked @Override fails to compile.
**Repair:** equals(Object) with @Override is a real override, so the HashSet will keep one Circle(1).
examples.result: Polymorphic calls behave as intended, and signature mistakes can't hide.

examples.title: The static that didn't dispatch
examples.situation: `Shape s = new Circle(2); s.kind()` returns "shape", and the learner expected "circle".
walkthrough: Static methods belong to the class and aren't dispatched on the object.
The call is resolved from the declared type Shape.
Make kind an instance method with @Override if it should vary by object.
examples.result: Each object now reports its own kind.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Every same-named member uses dynamic dispatch, including fields, static methods, overloads, and constructor calls.
misconceptions.correction: Only overridden instance methods dispatch on the runtime class. Overloads, static methods and fields are resolved at compile time from declared types.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The static that didn't dispatch", why did kind() return shape?

analogy.example: Dynamic dispatch is like **calling a phone number that forwards to whoever currently holds the role**: dial "the Shape", and the Circle actually answers in its own voice. Static methods are **a printed directory entry**: you get whatever was listed under the name you looked up, regardless of who's really there.
usefulFor: remembering forwarded calls vs printed directory
@Override = confirming the forwarding is set up
limitations: Phone forwarding can fail silently; @Override makes failures loud.
Overloads are chosen by the directory too: compile time.

nearTransfer.prompt: Given Animal with speak() and a static create(), and Dog overriding speak() and hiding create(), predict the output of calls through an Animal reference to a Dog. Check by running.

farTransfer.prompt: Find and fix three accidental non-overrides in a small codebase (a misspelled method, a wrong parameter type, a narrower access modifier). Add @Override everywhere relevant and show the compiler errors that would have caught each.
scaffold: Search for methods matching base names.

remediation.explanation: On every method meant to override, **write @Override**. When tracing a call, ask: **is it an overridden instance method (runtime class) or an overload, static or field (declared type)?**
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The static that didn't dispatch".

recap.summary: To trace polymorphic calls, remember overridden instance methods run the version from the object's runtime class, while overloads, static methods and fields are resolved from declared types at compile time, and mark every intended override with @Override so signature mistakes become compile errors.
